newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein frees Jordan bread riot detainees.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein frees Jordan bread riot detainees.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein on Tuesday declared a general amnesty for detainees arrested in connection with widespread bread riots in August.
The state news agency Petra said the king's amnesty also covered prisoners not considered a threat to public security or whose time in prison was considered sufficient.

"We request you to take measures to halt prosecution of those who deviated from the right way and harmed their country...in the events connected with the change in the wheat subsidies," Petra quoted the king as instructing Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti in a letter.

Human rights organisers welcomed the amnesty, which had been predicted ahead of the king's 61st birthday on Thursday and next week's opening of parliament. But they called for the king to change legislation which they said gave authorities too much power.
The king's letter gave no indication how many people were covered by the amnesty.
Government officials said hundreds of people were arrested after the rioting, the worst civil unrest in Jordan for seven years. But they said most were subsequently released.
"We don't have exact figures," said Labib Kamhawi, vice president of the Arab Organisation for Human Rights in Jordan.

"Our information is that 19 of those detained directly as a result of the rioting are still in detention," he said. "Other detainess are being held on 'criminal charges' that are basically political, like slander."

Tuesday's amnesty follows the king's release last Friday of leading critic Leith Shubailat, who was jailed in March for three years for denouncing the monarch as a traitor for his 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
King Hussein personally drove Shubailat home from prison.

"We do welcome these pardons, although we would like to see this as beginning a process, not an isolated effort," Kamhawi said. "It must mean putting an end to officials being able to violate rights of people."

The AOHR has sharply criticised Jordan's human rights record since Kabariti took office in February, accusing the government of torture and intimidation to stifle opposition to unpopular policies. The government denies the allegations.

Kabariti's decision to cut bread subsidies in August and introduce cash benefits for Jordan's poorest people virtually doubled the price of bread overnight. Demonstrations broke out in the southern town of Karak and spread to parts of Amman.
The king on Tuesday instructed Kabariti to "look again at the sale price of bread" in light of the fall in world grain prices from their record levels earlier this year, Petra said.
